questions.text: A pilot plans a 150-nautical-mile cross-country VFR flight departing in one hour. Which regulation specifically requires the pilot to obtain weather reports and forecasts before this flight?

options.label: A
options.text: 14 CFR 91.155, which establishes the Basic VFR weather minimums a pilot must comply with before and during any VFR flight in controlled airspace

options.label: B
options.text: 14 CFR 91.103, which requires the PIC to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight — including weather reports and forecasts — before any flight not in the vicinity of an airport

options.label: C
options.text: 14 CFR 91.7, which requires the PIC to determine that the aircraft is airworthy before flight and extends this determination to include the prevailing meteorological conditions along the route

options.label: D
options.text: 14 CFR 91.205, which specifies the required instruments and equipment for VFR flight and implicitly requires weather verification to determine whether VFR conditions exist at altitude

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 (Preflight Action) is the explicit regulatory source of the weather briefing requirement. It mandates that before beginning a flight, the PIC must become familiar with 'all available information' concerning that flight — and for any flight not in the vicinity of an airport, this specifically includes weather reports and forecasts. 91.155 establishes VFR minimums but does not require obtaining a briefing. 91.205 governs equipment requirements, not preflight actions. 91.7 is the airworthiness responsibility regulation and does not extend to weather briefing obligations.

questions.text: A private pilot uses a consumer smartphone weather application to check conditions before a cross-country flight. The app shows 'Partly Cloudy, 5 mph winds.' The pilot departs and encounters IFR conditions 40 miles en route. Has the pilot complied with 14 CFR 91.103?

options.label: A
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.103 requires obtaining aviation-specific weather information from official sources; a consumer app lacks cloud bases in AGL, PIREPs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, and other aviation-critical elements required for a compliant preflight briefing

options.label: B
options.text: No — 14 CFR 91.103 specifically prohibits the use of any digital application for preflight weather and requires a voice briefing from a certificated Flight Service Station meteorologist

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — 14 CFR 91.103 requires obtaining weather information, not a specific type of weather report; any source that provides current atmospheric conditions satisfies the regulation

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — consumer applications that aggregate National Weather Service data are considered approved sources under 14 CFR 91.103, provided the underlying government data is accessible within the app

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 requires familiarity with 'all available information' for the flight, which the FAA interprets as requiring aviation-specific data from official or approved sources. Consumer applications do not provide: cloud ceilings reported in AGL, prevailing visibility in statute miles, PIREPs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, NOTAMs, winds aloft at aviation altitudes, or freezing levels. The pilot has not satisfied 91.103. The position that any weather source suffices is incorrect. The claim that a consumer app becomes an approved source merely by aggregating NWS data mischaracterizes the approval mechanism — AC 91-78 and AC 91-92 govern EFB approval; consumer apps are not approved under these ACs simply by aggregating some NWS data. The claim that 91.103 prohibits any digital application is overbroad — digital sources including EFBs and AviationWeather.gov ARE approved under applicable ACs.

questions.text: A pilot obtained a Standard Briefing at 0600Z for a 0900Z departure. Convective development has been rapid. Before departure, the pilot calls FSS and says, 'I already have a briefing — I just need to know if any new SIGMETs or Convective SIGMETs have been issued along Whiskey-12 since 0600Z.' Which briefing type does this describe?

options.label: A
options.text: An Emergency Briefing — FSS reserves this designation for time-critical requests where the pilot faces an imminent departure under marginal or rapidly changing conditions

options.label: B
options.text: An Abbreviated Briefing — the pilot is supplementing a previously obtained Standard Briefing by requesting specific updated information rather than a complete re-briefing

options.label: C
options.text: An Outlook Briefing — the pilot is planning ahead for future weather conditions and requesting a forecast of expected SIGMET issuance beyond the current observation period

options.label: D
options.text: A Standard Briefing — any contact with FSS requesting weather information constitutes a Standard Briefing regardless of how much information the pilot requests

questions.explanation: AC 91-92 defines an Abbreviated Briefing as one used to supplement previously obtained mass-disseminated data, update a prior Standard Briefing, or request only specific items of information. The pilot already has a comprehensive Standard Briefing and is calling to request specific updated advisories — the textbook definition of an Abbreviated Briefing. The pilot should inform the FSS specialist that they have an existing briefing and specify exactly what additional information is needed. An Outlook Briefing is only appropriate when the departure is 6 or more hours in the future. Labeling this request an Emergency Briefing invents a category that does not exist in AC 91-92.

questions.text: According to AC 91-92, what is the correct first step in conducting a Standard Briefing when planning a cross-country flight?

options.label: A
options.text: Check the TAFs for departure and destination airports first — terminal forecasts establish the bookend conditions for the flight and determine whether VFR is achievable at both ends before reviewing en route data

options.label: B
options.text: Review the Surface Analysis Chart first — the broad synoptic picture from the chart provides the foundational context needed to properly interpret all subsequent weather products in the briefing sequence

options.label: C
options.text: Check Winds Aloft first — knowing the fuel burn and headwind component is critical for calculating fuel reserves, which determines whether alternate airport planning is required under 91.103

options.label: D
options.text: Review Adverse Conditions first — SIGMETs, AIRMETs, Convective SIGMETs, and TFRs must be assessed immediately to determine whether the flight is fundamentally unsafe before any other briefing elements are considered

questions.explanation: AC 91-92 specifies the Standard Briefing sequence as: Adverse Conditions → Synopsis → Current Conditions → En Route Forecasts → Destination Forecast → Winds Aloft → NOTAMs. Adverse Conditions (SIGMETs, AIRMETs, Convective SIGMETs, TFRs) must be reviewed first because they represent conditions that may make the entire flight fundamentally unsafe regardless of what any other briefing element shows. Checking the TAFs or Winds Aloft before adverse conditions risks spending time on irrelevant information when an active SIGMET would immediately cancel the flight. Reviewing the Surface Analysis Chart first reflects a reasonable meteorological approach but is not the AC 91-92 prescribed sequence.

questions.text: A pilot is planning a cross-country flight departing at 1400L. At 1100L, they open ForeFlight to conduct a weather briefing. Which statement best describes ForeFlight's status as a weather source under FAA guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: ForeFlight is an approved Electronic Flight Bag application under AC 91-78 when it sources its meteorological data directly from FAA and NWS feeds and satisfies the information requirements of 14 CFR 91.103

options.label: B
options.text: ForeFlight is not an approved source — all weather briefings for Part 91 operations must be obtained directly from the Leidos FSS website or by calling 1-800-WX-BRIEF to obtain a voice briefing from a specialist

options.label: C
options.text: ForeFlight is conditionally approved — it may be used for weather briefing only after the pilot has first obtained a baseline Standard Briefing from 1-800-WX-BRIEF within the preceding 4 hours

options.label: D
options.text: ForeFlight is approved only for supplemental use — it may display weather data during flight but may not be used for the preflight planning briefing required by 14 CFR 91.103 prior to departure

questions.explanation: AC 91-78 (Use of Class 1 or Class 2 Electronic Flight Bag) and AC 91-92 collectively establish the framework for EFB weather briefing approval. ForeFlight and similar applications are approved for use as a preflight briefing tool when they source data from FAA and NWS official feeds and provide the complete information categories required by 91.103 (adverse conditions, current conditions, forecasts, NOTAMs, and winds aloft). The key is that the underlying data must originate from official government sources — the platform may be commercial but the data pipeline must be authoritative. Treating ForeFlight as unapproved incorrectly restricts legitimate EFBs. Requiring a prior baseline briefing within 4 hours, or limiting it to in-flight display only rather than preflight briefing, both invent restrictions that do not exist in the applicable ACs.

questions.text: A student mentions to their CFI that they 'checked DUATS before the flight.' What is the accurate response regarding DUATS?

options.label: A
options.text: DUATS is still an approved FAA weather source — it was relaunched in 2021 as a backup system for Flight Service Station outages and remains an authorized preflight briefing resource

options.label: B
options.text: DUATS is valid for weather data but not for NOTAMs — pilots using DUATS must supplement it with a separate NOTAM check from the FAA PilotWeb portal before the briefing is considered complete

options.label: C
options.text: DUATS is still operational but is now only available to certificated instrument-rated pilots logging official IFR currency under 14 CFR 61.57 requirements

options.label: D
options.text: DUATS was discontinued by the FAA in 2018 — its replacement is Leidos Flight Service accessible via 1800wxbrief.com or 1-800-WX-BRIEF; referencing DUATS on a checkride indicates outdated training material

questions.explanation: The FAA terminated the DUATS (Direct User Access Terminal Service) contract in 2018. Leidos Flight Service (1800wxbrief.com / 1-800-WX-BRIEF) is the current official FAA-contracted Flight Service provider. A pilot or student who references DUATS during a checkride reveals training from outdated materials — this is a direct signal to the DPE that the applicant has not kept their weather briefing knowledge current. Approved study sources including AC 91-92 and the current edition of the Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) reflect this transition. All options except C describe operational states of DUATS that do not exist.

questions.text: You are planning a 120-mile VFR cross-country. Your running late and your passengers are waiting. You check the local news weather app which shows 'Mostly Sunny, nice day.' You feel the conditions look good outside. What is the SAFEST action before departure?

options.label: A
options.text: Take a quick look at the radar on your smartphone weather app and depart if it shows no red cells — real-time radar eliminates the most dangerous weather hazard and constitutes a sufficient safety check for a VFR day flight

options.label: B
options.text: Cancel the flight entirely — departing late with passengers already waiting creates a toxic external pressure environment, and any flight under schedule pressure is statistically high-risk regardless of weather conditions

options.label: C
options.text: Obtain a complete Standard Briefing from AviationWeather.gov or 1800wxbrief.com before departure — external pressure and sunny skies do not eliminate the obligation to verify AIRMETs, SIGMETs, winds aloft, and NOTAMs that may affect the flight

options.label: D
options.text: Depart — the visual conditions look acceptable and you can self-evaluate the sky far better than any digital product; a news weather app for context plus your own windshield assessment satisfies the spirit of 91.103

questions.explanation: A consumer weather app and a visual scan of the sky satisfy neither the regulatory requirement of 14 CFR 91.103 nor the safety standard of a complete preflight briefing. 'Mostly Sunny' on a news app does not tell you about an AIRMET Sierra for mountain obscuration 60 miles ahead, a TFR over your route, or a NOTAM closing your destination runway. Departing on your own visual read of the sky is Macho — treating the pilot's visual assessment as superior to a documented, comprehensive official briefing. Glancing at smartphone radar and launching if no red cells appear is Get-There-Itis — minimizing the briefing requirement to the single most obvious hazard (visible convection) while ignoring all other flight-critical data. Cancelling the flight outright is Resignation — external pressure is a real risk factor, but it does not require cancellation; it requires professional discipline to complete an adequate briefing before departure. Reference: AC 91-92 documents that the majority of fatal VFR-into-IMC accidents involve pilots who conducted no aviation-specific weather briefing.
questions.sjt_rationale: Launching on a visual read is Macho — self-assessment substituted for regulatory compliance. A quick radar glance then departing is Get-There-Itis — checking the minimum that allows departure rationalization. Cancelling the flight is Resignation — treating external pressure as an automatic disqualifier rather than a factor to manage. The complete Standard Briefing is the only response that complies with 91.103 AND demonstrates professional ADM.

questions.text: During a checkride oral, the DPE asks: 'Walk me through the weather briefing you obtained for today.' The applicant obtained a briefing on ForeFlight but does not remember reviewing adverse conditions or NOTAMs. They recall checking the destination TAF and winds aloft. The weather looks fine. What is the SAFEST response?

options.label: A
options.text: Request the DPE reschedule the practical test for tomorrow to allow adequate time to complete a proper briefing — any checkride that begins with an incomplete preflight briefing must be postponed

options.label: B
options.text: Confidently state that the briefing was complete and the weather is good — the TAF and winds aloft are the most operationally relevant products and the DPE will accept a partial briefing for a clear-weather checkride day

options.label: C
options.text: Acknowledge to the DPE that the adverse conditions and NOTAM reviews were incomplete, request a brief pause to complete those checklist items now, then provide a complete AC 91-92 sequence walkthrough before proceeding

options.label: D
options.text: State that the weather is VMC so adverse condition advisories are unlikely to be active — SIGMETs and AIRMETs are only issued during weather events and can be skipped on clear-weather days without safety impact

questions.explanation: Acknowledging a gap and correcting it in real-time demonstrates exactly what the DPE is evaluating: situational awareness, intellectual honesty, and correct ADM. The FAA does not expect perfection — it expects professionalism. Completing the missing briefing elements (adverse conditions and NOTAMs) before the oral continues is the appropriate corrective action. Confidently claiming the briefing was complete is Macho — fabricating the completeness of a briefing to appear competent. This is an integrity failure in addition to a knowledge failure. Claiming SIGMETs and AIRMETs can be skipped on a clear-weather day is Invulnerability — 'nothing bad happens on clear days.' TFRs, runway closures (NOTAMs), and even SIGMETs for volcanic ash or military operations exist regardless of local weather conditions. Requesting the DPE reschedule the test for tomorrow is Resignation — the briefing is quickly completable; postponing the entire test is disproportionate and demonstrates poor judgment.
questions.sjt_rationale: Claiming completeness is Macho — misrepresenting preparation to avoid admission of error. Skipping advisories on a clear day is Invulnerability — assuming adverse conditions cannot exist in clear weather. Requesting a reschedule is Resignation — treating a correctable gap as an insurmountable obstacle. Owning and completing the gap is honest, professional, and operationally correct.
